name: Wan 3.0
tagline: Web app that runs Alibaba's Wan video model for you and sells generations by credit.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The Wan family of video models has open weights, so nothing about the generation itself is a secret this site owns. What it sells is a queue, a GPU fleet, and a text box you do not have to install, which is a real service even if it is a thin one. An agent can absolutely build you a local prompt-to-video queue with a job list, seeds, and an mp4 gallery in a weekend. The catch is inference: text-to-video at usable resolution wants a fat GPU and patience, and if you rent one you have re-created a smaller, worse version of what you were paying for. Build it if you already own the hardware or generate enough clips to care about per-credit pricing.
coreLoopDIY: A local web UI that takes a prompt, queues it against a locally loaded Wan text-to-video pipeline, and drops finished mp4 files into a browsable gallery with the seed and settings attached.
requirements: An NVIDIA GPU with a lot of VRAM, or a rented GPU box billed by the hour
Model weights downloaded locally (tens of GB)
Tolerance for multi-minute renders and out-of-memory errors
whatYouLose: Instant results: their fleet parallelizes, your single card does not
Whatever prompt presets, resolution ladders, and upscale or audio passes they bolted on top
Free upgrades when a new model version lands, and someone else's job tuning it
Generating anything from your phone without exposing a home server
A support channel when the pipeline breaks after a dependency bump
moatNotes: The GPU fleet is the product. The model underneath is open weights that anyone, including you, can download.
whyPeopleStillPay: Video inference is the rare workload where renting genuinely beats owning for most people. A card that renders Wan clips at a tolerable speed costs more than years of credits, sits idle between sessions, and needs a person who enjoys debugging CUDA. Paying per clip converts a hardware purchase plus a hobby into a line item, and hosted wrappers also absorb the churn every time the upstream model changes shape. The value is convenience and amortized silicon, not cleverness.
notes: Unofficial wrapper around open-weight Wan models, so the only thing you cannot clone is the hardware bill.
prompt:
Build a local text-to-video studio for open-weight Wan models. Single machine, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn
- diffusers plus torch with CUDA for inference
- SQLite via sqlite3 for the job table
- One static index.html with vanilla JS and fetch polling, no build step
- ffmpeg via subprocess for frame-to-mp4 encoding

Behavior:
- POST /jobs accepts prompt, negative_prompt, num_frames, fps, steps, guidance, seed (null means random) and inserts a row with status queued
- A single background worker thread processes jobs one at a time, FIFO, loading the pipeline once and keeping it resident
- Job statuses: queued, running, done, failed. Store the error string on failure
- Finished videos land in ./outputs/{job_id}.mp4 alongside a {job_id}.json with every setting and the resolved seed
- GET /jobs returns the list newest first, GET /outputs serves the files
- UI: prompt box, collapsible advanced settings, a queue list that polls every 2 seconds, and a gallery of finished clips with inline video players and a "reuse settings" button that refills the form

Rules:
- Model id or local weights path comes from .env (MODEL_PATH, DEVICE, DTYPE). Ship .env.example, never hardcode paths
- On startup, log VRAM available and fail loudly with a readable message if the model cannot load
- Support offload flags for low-VRAM cards, read from .env
- Out of scope: users, auth, billing, image-to-video, upscaling, audio, multi-GPU, remote API fallbacks
- README with exact install commands, the weights download step, and a note that a first render may take many minutes
